prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock based on magic-wavelength trapping and its development to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I move my preferred configuration from B022 to B012. In round 1 I put twisted bilayer graphene first because it is a clean mechanism (the Bistritzer-MacDonald interference argument) that predicted where to look, and I still think the existence of flat bands and correlated insulators is settled. What changed is the weight I give to exact credit and to what the committee can defend in public. The optical lattice clock is also a simple mechanism: the magic wavelength cancels the first-order light shift, so thousands of atoms can be interrogated without Doppler or recoil shifts, and the remaining systematics can be accounted for in physical detail. It has been reproduced and surpassed by independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) for about twenty years. The two-name credit is the cleanest on the shortlist, with Katori for the concept and first demonstration and Ye for taking it to the accuracy frontier, including the many-body and spin-resolved clock physics. All eight members ranked it at opening and no one opposes it on merit. I would word the citation narrowly around the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 regime, and leave the fundamental-physics payoff (varying constants, dark matter, redshift tests, redefinition of the second) out of the citation, since none of these is realised yet.
statement.case_against: The honest weakness is novelty. The 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize cover much of the enabling machinery, and a sceptic can call the lattice clock a decisive refinement of a recognised program rather than a new phenomenon. Single-ion clocks reached comparable accuracy by another route. Credit also extends beyond two names: Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Hinkley, Bloom and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups made real contributions, and I cannot judge priority in that community from my own field. By comparison, B022 opens a new class of phenomena, and I think it will deserve a prize in a few years once the pairing question is better understood; B012 is the safer choice now, not the more exciting one.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock is a verified measurement advance: the magic wavelength removes light shift, Doppler and recoil effects, independent laboratories agree at 10^-18, and Katori and Ye form a clean pair without stretching the three-person limit.
responses.response: I agree with the physics and the attribution point, and it is the main reason I moved. Where you and I differ is how much of the fundamental-physics payoff belongs in the citation. I would not include it, because no variation of constants or dark-matter signal has been seen and the second has not been redefined. The narrow wording you propose (invention and development, 10^-18 fractional uncertainty) is enough. My residual worry is the one you raise yourself: the earlier comb and ion prizes. I think the answer to the chair's first question is that the lattice clock is the first scheme that combines a large atomic ensemble with a first-order insensitivity to the trapping field. That is a distinct mechanism, not simply a better comb or a better ion, and the citation should say so.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp topological insulator as a mature theory-plus-experiment case and says he would accept B012 if topological matter fails to reach agreement.
responses.response: I still regard B018 as scientifically strong and I keep it as my second alternative. But I think the round-1 record answers the chair's question on it. The attribution problem is real: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe as the host, Zhang is deceased, and the three-dimensional Fu-Kane-Mele strand cannot be fitted into three names. The 2016 prize also covers much of the conceptual ground. I think your own stated willingness to accept B012 is the sensible place for us to meet. This is a judgment about what can be credited without a visible omission, not a view that B018 is a weaker piece of physics.

responses.point: Johansson calls magic-angle graphene 'a bit early' because the pairing mechanism is unsettled, and has moved from circuit QED to B012 while flagging a possible recusal if superconducting-circuit candidates advance.
responses.response: I answered your 'a bit early' remark in round 1 by saying that flat bands and correlated insulators do not depend on the pairing mechanism. I still hold that as physics, but I accept that the committee does not need to settle that dispute now, because Yuan Cao and the early confirming groups are also outside the credited trio and the pairing question will probably not be resolved soon. I welcome that you left B064 out of your configuration and note your recusal flag. On B012 I take your point that the attribution is clean, but I would ask you to say whether you think Katori and Ye adequately represent priority within the lattice-clock community, since you work next to experimentalists in a neighbouring field.

responses.point: Olsson prefers aberration-corrected electron optics, acknowledges that Knut Urban is omitted and that her own field may bias her, and names B012 as her most acceptable fallback.
responses.response: Thank you for stating the field-closeness openly. My own question in round 1 stands: it is not clear to me that instrument invention counts as a discovery in physics under the will, and the Rose-Haider-Krivanek split omits Urban, who led the first corrected TEM with Haider and Rose. Your fallback to B012 is also the position I now hold, so the practical disagreement between us has largely gone. If the committee wants to consider a second part for a future year, I would still like to understand what the decisive contribution of each of the three was.

uncertainties: Whether Katori and Ye adequately represent priority within the lattice-clock community given Lemonde, Ludlow, Takamoto, Bloom and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups; an expert report from the clock community would help.
Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as distinct enough from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether a prize now for B012 forecloses B022 later, or whether B022 stays available in a few years once the pairing mechanism is clearer.
I am a statistical physicist and cannot judge the experimental detail of the atomic and precision-measurement community myself.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict has changed since round 1. I have no listed collaboration, institutional tie or supervision relation with Katori, Ye or any other credited name on the shortlist. I am at the University of Gothenburg, which is in the same environment as Johansson and Olsson at Chalmers, but I have no specific collaboration with either of them that bears on B012. I defer to colleagues on the experimental detail of the atomic, particle and astroparticle candidates.
